response: Certainly, here is my answer: Out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words present a significant challenge in today's large vocabulary continuous speech recognition (LVCSR) systems. OOV words, by definition, are words that are absent from the dictionary of a speech recognizer and can lead to drastically reduced system performance if not properly handled. OOV words can cause recognition failures, which may propagate through a speech recognition pipeline and significantly impair the performance of downstream applications such as speech-to-text and text-to-speech systems, as well as voice-controlled interfaces. Traditionally, OOV detection in LVCSR is treated as a binary classification problem where each word (or small region) in a recognized transcript is classified as either in-vocabulary (IN) or out-of-vocabulary (OOV). State-of-the-art OOV detection methods typically rely on local information, such as phonetic context, acoustic features from the speech signal, or language modeling scores. However, these methods often have limitations. Phonetic information can be incomplete, acoustics features can be highly dependent on the speaking environment, and language modeling scores can be skewed due to the uncertainty inherent in recognition. As a result, these methods may struggle to accurately detect OOV regions, particularly when words are short or are phonetically similar to known words. A key observation is that OOV detection could potentially benefit from contextual information. An example of such an ontology is WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998), which, though successful, suffers from several questions such as the domain coverage and the accuracy and completeness of the attributes and relations encoded. One way to extend the ontology with attributes and relations (which we will simply call attributes) is to manually add them to the structure. However, this can be time-consuming and is not scalable. Alternatively, a possibility is to automatically generate attributes based on word usage, using corpus counts. For example, one can count how often the word "dog" occurs with features such as "hairy" or "fawn" and then add those as attributes to WordNet. This simple approach ignores several issues such as the required frequency thresholds, importance of context features, and how attribute attachment is performed, which limits the effectiveness and accuracy of inferred attributes. We leverage Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA; Blei et al., 2003) and its variants, as well as related shallow probabilistic models specifically designed for this task. The proposed methods can automatically label concepts in a KB with a substantial set of attributes (e.g., features, properties, or relationships). The proposed methods are evaluated along two dimensions: the precision of the ranked lists of attributes as provided, and the quality of the attribute assignments in practice, as judged by expert annotations or domain understanding. response: Automated Essay Scoring (AES) is one of the key applications in natural language processing. AES systems today still rely heavily on carefully designed features to evaluate and score essays. These features include features related to length, vocabulary, grammatical correctness, and more. However, the ideal set of features is not only difficult to design, but also may vary depending on questions or topics asked. In this paper, we explore an alternative to feature-based AES systems. Instead of designing features, we let the machine learn a useful representation of essays and their scores directly from the word sequence itself. We use Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), especially Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, to achieve this, as they are powerful models for sequential data. By training such models, we learn how to map features of essays (which are just word sequences) to scores directly, without any semantic features. The main benefits of this approach are \begin{enumerate} \item No need for painstaking handcrafted features; \item The ability to learn various patterns and features from data automatically, as the model learns from data how to assign scores to essays. \end{enumerate} In this work we report on this approach, including experiments for achieving the best performance, and discuss some insights on the learned models. We perform a comparison with a strong baseline system that uses a wide range of handcrafted features to evaluate essays. Our models show improved performance over the baseline on a corpus designed for automated essay scoring, with the best model yielding a 5.6% improvement on a widely used metric called Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK), without any manual feature engineering. To set the stage for our work, we in Section 2 present an overview of existing AES systems and the benefits and challenges of feature-based systems and some related neural approaches. Section 3 describes our neural approach in detail and the different models we experimented with. In Section 4 we provide an experimental setup, including the data and evaluation metrics used. Section 5 presents our experimental results and measured improvements over a strong baseline. We also conduct some analyses to gain deeper insights into how our LSTM-based system works. For instance, we use layer-wise relevance propagation (LReLU) to understand which words in an essay contribute most to changing the predicted score. Feature engineering for AES often requires a deep understanding of English writing evaluation criteria that are not easily translated into computer code for automation. For instance, features like "Sentence complexity" or "Grammar accuracy" might be useful but require real expertise to capture effectively. Our approach avoids most of these difficulties by learning those relationships directly from data. This work demonstrates the potential power of neural machine learning in addressing complex and subtle natural language problems like automated essay scoring. It also points to the possibility of further fine-tuning our models to particular datasets or constraints, which could be achieved through more careful tuning and specific data requirements, or through exploring more complex neural architectures. We hope that our findings will be useful not just for auto-grading, but also for broader applications in natural language understanding and text analysis. Finally, we discuss the limitations of our approach and future directions in Section 6. Temporal information extraction from natural language text has been a challenging research problem for various applications, including question answering (QA). Many tasks in QA, such as determining when an event happened, who questions, or when a particular entity was involved in an event, rely heavily on the ability of a system to extract and reason about temporal relations from text. Typically, temporal information extraction systems perform two independent tasks: (1) identifying temporal expressions or temporal relations in text and (2) extracting temporal information (such as time points or durations) from those expressions. However, such approaches often have to contend with complex linguistic phenomena, such as tense, aspect, and event ordering, which can lead to ambiguity or uncertainty in determining relationships among semantic entities. These challenges become particularly pressing in the context of QA, where the demand for precise answers often necessitates extracting and understanding complex temporal relations quickly and accurately. Moreover, QA systems are sometimes required to handle temporal relations both within a sentence (e.g., "When was the first Beatles song recorded?") and across sentences or between multiple referential objects (e.g., "What was the last novel written by this author before he began this series?"). The problem of temporal relation extraction for QA has been specifically addressed by researchers through the QA-TempEval task of the SemEval 2015 workshop (Guo et al., 2015), which challenges systems to determine temporal relations between entities mentioned in questions (QA pairs). This task requires systems to go beyond mere text-based temporal expression identification; they must derive and reason about the temporal relationship between a question entity and a candidate answer entity through a broad analysis of the text. A promising approach for addressing this challenge involves leveraging deep learning techniques, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, which can capture the sequential characteristics of language and the long-range dependencies in textual data. However, the application of LSTMs for temporal information extraction in the context of QA is still in its early stages, and existing methods often suffer limitations in performance and adaptability to diverse QA scenarios. response: Transliteration, the process of converting text from one script (e.g. Latin, Arabic, Cyrillic) to another, is a key factor in cross-lingual NLP applications. It allows for example the integration of texts in various scripts within a single machine translation system (Prochaska and Mooney, 2010;Sénéchal et al., 2008) or for information retrieval and question answering systems (Klein and Manning, 2002). Transliteration can also be utilized to build parallel word lists (Koehn and Monz, 2006). While it is a relatively well-understood problem in the industry, with mature solutions available in most web search engines, academia continues to address the problem by introducing more sophisticated techniques. Transliteration mining is the process by which transliterations between two languages are automatically derived from comparable or parallel texts (such as English - Arabic). Most existing approaches to this problem use purely corpus-based techniques (e.g. n-gram based language models) or standard techniques for word alignment such as GIZA++ (Och and Ney, 2003). GIZA++ is an application of IBM Model 1 (Brown et al., 1993), a uniform context model for word alignment. When applying GIZA++ to different character-based languages with shallow structures (e.g. Indian, while the Arabic script benefits from deeper structure in the case of medium-sized corpora), it often exhibits suboptimal performance. More recent techniques deviate from the n-gram (or word-based) context model (e.g., Yang et al., 2012;Sakaguchi et al., 2013). Algorithms inspired by the work on character-based and subword-level language model analysis (Bengio et al., 2003;Joshi et al., 2007;Santos et al., 2014) have the potential to improve transliteration mining, especially for those script pairs that exhibit complex, context-dependent transliteration rules. However, none of these proposals specifically dealt with the graph-theoretic nature of transliteration relations between languages. Specifically, given an initial set of transliteration mappings provided by human annotators or by automatic alignment (e.g., GIZA++), it is often possible to infer additional mappings for unseen character sequences by leveraging previously established ones. response: Training high-quality classifiers often requires large amounts of annotated training data. However, acquiring such data is cost prohibitive or nearly impossible; these are two primary motivations for active learning which aims at reducing the cost of annotation while preserving the quality of the resulting classifiers (Seung, 1999;Cohn and Alm, 2000;Settles , 2010). Specifically, active learning aims to reduce the total number of examples that need to be annotated by exploiting the capacity of the learner to actually select those examples that are most informative to the underlying label set. The utility of active learning keeps coming up due to successes in a range of applications (Frosst et al., 2010;Whiteley et al., 2011;Tomasulo and Bethard, 2014;Casiez et al., 2015). As the sample of data grows larger, the total required annotation effort, however, can be still quite substantial and cost prohibitive, which motivates exploring its potential in combination with crowdsourcing. Crowdsourcing offers a large pool of workers at a relatively low cost (Crowston and Fagnot, 2013), opening up the possibility of tackling much larger scale annotation efforts than would be possible through traditional routes. Despite this opportunity, however, these two approaches have not been combined successfully to date. Indeed, incorporating active learning while exploiting crowdsourcing benefits comes with its own sets of challenges. The main challenge to the adoption of active learning in the crowdsourcing context arises from the inherent noise (Peysakhovich and Ryabinin, 2011;Odland et al., 2011) and variability (Singh and Anand, 2014;Rzeszotarski and Kittur, 2015) that are typically inconsistent across different sources of crowdsourced work. The excessive noise makes it difficult to design or apply active learning methods since different sources (tasks or contexts measured in terms of worker demographics or just the time of the day) often produce different performance levels on the same task (Nonnecke et al., 2000;Karger et al., 2008). Moreover, changing the set of workers working on a particular task might also modify the actual underlying distribution of the data, which again is not easily predicted in complex/personalized tasks such as image classification. Due to these challenges, the majority of the existing work remains focused on evaluating active learning in contexts that are devoid of such variability, and even when the variability is present, much work has centered around mitigation strategies for the effect of noise (Karger et al., 2008;Kittur et al., 2018;Harris et al., 2016). These problems include, but are not limited to, the prediction of biological processes (Ashburner et al., 2000), protein function (Troyanskaya et al., 2001), and the recognition of natural language patterns (Chieu and Ng, 2002;Tsochantaridis et al., 2005;Bui et al., 2009). One essential feature of TK-based approaches is their ability to represent complex hierarchical structures in a computationally efficient way by first mapping these features into a numerical feature space. A typical choice is to use Fischer kernels (Bai and Lai, 1982;Pfahringer et al., 1995) which allow the computation of certain similarity metrics between trees, known as tree kernels (Przepiórkowski, 2005). Despite their practical success, TK methods lack interpretability and transparency. As a result, it's often difficult to gain any insights or understand the decision-making process that a TK-based model uses. One side effect of this lack of interpretability is that different training data or even initial conditions during training may result in significantly altered model performance, making these models harder to interpret and less reliable over time. Another issue with TKs is computational overhead. As they can have high computational complexity (e.g., O(n³) for matching two trees), they significantly slow down training time. This is a major obstacle when trying to scale to larger datasets or longer feature trees, and it restricts the amount and type of learning we can perform. Given these challenges, it is desirable to find a way to better understand the input features that influence the decisions of a TK-based model. In this work, we focus on mining inference formulas from KB data, which involve a series of steps to questions or modify the KB entries. This process is vital for updating and extending the KB itself, and for real-world applications like question answering and inference-based decision support systems. While KBs are expanding rapidly (e.g., WordNet , Freebase , and even larger graph-structured KBs like DBpedia and knowledge graphs based on industry, health, etc.), there is a pressing need for efficient inference methods that can generate and validate new formulas automatically. Accurate and contextually relevant categorized data can make a significant difference in the quality and speed of decision-making for clinicians, researchers, and patients alike. Currently, many systems use keyword matching, domain-specific taxonomies, or simplistic schemes that fail to fully capture the complexity and nuances of medical information categorizations. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a Medical Product Category Hierarchy (MEDOI) designed to provide a more structured and contextually informed approach to categorizing medical products. Our research questions were: 1. What benefits can a comprehensive and contextual medical product hierarchy bring to the process of information organization and retrieval? 2. How can we design a system that learns from and adapts to user interaction for better performance and handling of ambiguity in medical product categorization? To answer these questions, we first identified potential hierarchical structures and proposed MEDOI's modular structure which consists of both general and domain-specific levels. For general categorization, we leveraged and expanded existing taxonomies like SNOMED-CT and the United States Pharmacopeia (USP), while for domain-specific details, we integrated in-vitro data acquisition and clinical application-specific frameworks to provide richer context. This multi-faceted approach enables MEDOI to capture both broader, high-level categorizations as well as highly granular, domain-specific product subtypes. We then investigated user interaction as a learning mechanism to enhance MEDOI's performance and automate some aspects of product categorization that might be ambiguous or less likely to be properly tagged (e.g., colloquial terms for products that have different professional names or finding the most relevant category for a product with multiple or evolving uses). To achieve this, we implemented a Bayesian framework for MEDOI that allows continuous refining of product category assignment based on user feedback. response: Training natural language processing (NLP) algorithms reliably on large datasets of annotated text requires an enormous amount of manual labor. Even for well-studied languages such as English, the annotation of large corpora with comprehensive linguistic features is unrealistic. Moreover, annotation of complex features such as discourse structure typically requires particular expertise, which further limits the number of experts willing to engage in manual annotation. Crowdsourcing has emerged as an efficient and effective way to rapidly develop large annotated corpora, with studies showing that (1) language annotation can be effectively crowdsourced (Adiwardana et al., 2017; Callison-Burch, 2009; Gurulingappa et al., 2012; Verga et al., 2017), and (2) that crowdsourced annotations can be just as reliable as those provided by expert annotators (Adiwardana et al., 2017; Gurulingappa et al., 2012). However, crowd-based annotation processes are typically more complex than standard expert-only annotation workflows, and thus require careful design decisions to optimize efficiency and accuracy. One key design decision is whether or not to use multi-stage crowdsourcing. In single-stage crowdsourcing, each annotator is responsible for performing a given task from start to finish. In contrast, in multi-stage crowdsourcing different types of tasks are performed by different cohorts of workers, while the results of one stage can be used to guide the work in the next stage (Gurulingappa et al., 2012). An important advantage of multi-stage crowdsourcing for linguistic annotation is that it can significantly reduce the time required for annotators to complete each step, because for each step, they are provided with some partial information about what needs to be done and can thus plan their work more efficiently (Hovy et al., 2006; Verga et al., 2017). This reduced cognitive burden can make the task more appealing to a wider range of annotators, who may otherwise be put off by the difficulty of the task or by the time commitment required for a single task. However, multi-stage crowdsourcing can also be more challenging to design and implement, and it requires systematic planning to ensure that the changing task requirements and dependency structure are aligned with the workers' capabilities and knowledge. Annotations of more complex linguistic features are also notoriously more difficult to obtain from crowdsourcing due to the additional complexity of interpretation and the need for better tools to support the annotation process (Baldridge 2015; Bizzoni et al. 2015). One such complex feature is discourse structure. Discourse structure provides information about how sentences are organized within a larger unit of text (e.g., a paragraph or a conversation), typically including relations such as pragmatic connectives (for instance, however or summing up), coreference, and disjoint discourse relations (Schiffrin 1987; Knott 2009). While discourse structure is a relatively well-studied topic in terms of theory, manually annotating it requires significant expertise and time (e.g., it took several years of annotation effort to create the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) (Prasad et al. 2008)). Therefore, annotating discourse structure represents a significant challenge for crowdsourcing, both because of the complexity of the annotation task, and because annotation of discourse relations typically requires deeper understanding of the content of the text and its context. The main goal of this paper is to demonstrate the potential of crowdsourcing to rapidly and effectively create a large corpus annotated with discourse structure

However, "labeling" judgments that may require inference and minimal language comprehension can also be elicited with no noteworthy negative impact observed; and it can sometimes even be extracted from existing data through techniques like matrix factorization (MF) (e.g., to predict matrix entries). This observation creates alternative perspectives on the AL problem: instead of asking "Which examples to label?" we could ask "Which features to have labeled?" to decide on labeling among semantic features instead of whole instance-level sample from a collection. By making each feature as an individual to be judged and activated for labeling, this "feature-labeling" perspective requires re-evaluating the choice of instances, yet how instances are defined changes since the task now involves similar reasoning over various attributes of instances. As proposed in this paper, we refer to this general approach or problem as Actively Learning For Features (ALFF). In this problem, AL systems attempt to produce features presumed to have high enough "informative value" that labeling them assumedly minimizes the system's uncertainty about label decisions in entire instances the features belong to, within a model, or even on an ensemble level. Nevertheless, neural models can still learn meaningful features from small datasets. Significantly, recent work has shown that one indispensable ally for the development of neural models under this regime is artificial data augmentation. In scope with the domain of machine translation (MT), where parallel corpora can be sparse, a variety of data augmentation strategies have been proposed (Chiu and Ng, 2018;Tiedemann, 2012;Koehn and Knowles, 2017;Song et al., 2017). For MT in particular, augmenting training data can be viewed as a task of generating additional training examples from existing ones. This task shares commonalities with other natural language processing problems that involve exemplar-based generation, but from a specific perspective: the generated examples need to be linguistically plausible and have utility in the context of the task they augment, i.e., MT. From a computational angle, data augmentation techniques in the neural MT context have often been similar to approaches in image data manipulation: random noise or transformations are applied to input sentences, which presumably enriches the training set with new, yet still semantically plausible, variants of the input (Chiu and Ng, 2018;Song et al., 2017). However, these methods are in tension with the primary assumption of MT training: to learn plausible translations given an input sentence, and to do so without relying on explicit syntactic or semantic features (Denkowski and Lavie, 2014). Instead, they focus on surface-level phenomena, which can sometimes violate grammaticality or lexical usage (Chiu and Ng, 2018). Two core issues are at the heart of this problem. First, even though the goal is to learn to generate parses that lead to the given denotation (or answers), the search for candidate parses – which is typically done using the predictions from the current model itself – may not perform well enough, especially at the beginning of the learning process when the model is not accurate enough yet. Second, the choice of update rule to refine the model is also important. Here, we define “better” in a way that is compatible with language and text semantics. For instance, a good parse should satisfy both semantic correctness and reasonable syntactic structure. We can design a ranking function over the candidate parses. Candidate parses with high scores are expected to lead to more accurate learning and, while the system initially benefits from indirect supervision in learning, the acquisition of its own model allows to also align with the training data at a deeper level (e.g., syntactic structure). In recent years, the accelerated development of statistical machine translation (SMT) has led to deep neural network (DNN)-based sentence simplification methods, which learn internal rules from paired corpora. To address this, this paper explores a new framework that combines DNN models and external paraphrase rules for sentence simplification. Our idea is to jointly leverage the strength of a neural model and rule knowledge from an external paraphrase database. This is in line with the recent trend to augment neural models with knowledge graph-based or rule-based methods in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Our simplification model is based on a transformer architecture, a type of deep learning architecture that has been particularly successful in SMT and other sequence-to-sequence NLP tasks, including text summarization and question answering. Transformer models learn representations of input sequences through multi-head self-attention mechanisms, which enable them to model long-range dependencies and capture nuances in the context between sequential elements. However, these models lack the advantage of being pre-trained on a large, domain specific and task specific knowledge base such as SPPED (Simplification with Pre-training and Predefined Rules), while the latter suffers from the problem of in-vivo rule acquisition and its application to unseen examples, not to mention the engineering time and effort required to carefully design and test such rules. It is common to train multiple models and select the best one, but the best model may happen to be merely a lucky run. An essential aspect of assessing the performance and quality of these systems is through the evaluation and analysis of their generated summaries. A recent study (Paulus et al., 2017) demonstrated that current techniques for multi-document summarization, though effective, are mostly focused on data extracted from a single document. This limitation is a significant barrier to the development of truly adaptive and accurate multi-document summarizers. The complexity of creating such a dynamic system stems from several challenges. Firstly, in multi-document summarization, the system is required to identify semantic overlaps and redundant information across multiple documents, which requires a deep understanding of content and discourse relationships. Secondly, the system must ensure that the generated summary is coherent, relevant, and free from unnecessary information, while also preserving key details and relationships. Thirdly, the system should be able to abstract away from specific document structures and word forms, and generate summaries in a language that generalizes or extracts the core meaning across multiple documents. One common approach to tackling these issues is through the use of different levels of content representation. Traditional models often rely on summarization features such as word co-occurrence matrices, n-gram models, or even simple syntactic structures, which are derived from surface-level text characteristics. However, these representations often fall short in capturing deep semantic relationships or abstract meaning that are essential for summarization across different documents or domains. As a form of semantic representation, AMR captures meaning in a language-agnostic form, using a directed graph where nodes represent concepts and edges represent semantic relations. A key challenge of cQA systems is to index the large collection of questions and find relevant answers. Unlike standard search engines that mainly keeps track of keywords and content representation, cQA systems primarily need to identify questions, and then retrieve similar questions (with or without answers) in the form of closest pairs (Ren et al., 2005;Peng and Karypis, 2012;Nguyen, 2011). While identifying answerable questions and answering them properly have been widely studied (e.g., Kwok, 2000;John et al., 2005;Yuan et al., 2009;Li and Roth, 2002), the question detection and retrieval within or even across different cQA platforms have received scanty attention. Question detection, which is usually presumed as a trivial task in English corpus due to the heavy use of question marks and 'interrogative' markers in question sentences, often becomes a challenging task in cQA scenarios, where questions are framed informally (e.g., posts without formal punctuation), and without specific 'question markers'. The variety of ways to inquire about a same topic (e.g., "What?", "How?", "Does it?", etc.) also complicates the question detection task. It provides essential information about what language users are talking about, what they are committed to, and whether the intended meaning of various linguistic expressions can be influenced by the context in which they appear. response: Lexical cohesion, which describes the way in which words or phrases in a text work together to convey meaning, has long been considered essential for assessing and improving the overall readability and coherence of a document. It has traditionally been measured through techniques that focus on word repetition and organization (Halliday and Hasan, 1976;Satlow, 1984), which are useful for identifying basic patterns and potential areas where coherence and cohesion may be improved. These techniques often rely on simple metrics like “repetition of keywords” or fractal analysis (Adelman, 1977) that count how many times certain words or word forms recur. However, these measures do not always fully capture the nuanced nature of lexical cohesion, which can be more dynamic and context-dependent, or account for the various syntactical and rhetorical strategies authors employ to create relationships among semantic entities beyond simple word repetition. For example, cohesion can also be achieved through the use of synonyms, antonyms, hyponyms, hypernyms, and other lexical relationships, as well as through the use of anaphoric references, forward and backward referencing, and various stylistic and rhetorical devices. Thus, for achieving sophisticated analysis of linguistic cohesion within or even across documents, more sophisticated and contextually aware metrics are required. One particularly useful but under-explored aspect of lexical cohesion is the cognitive accessibility of referring expressions, the way in which the authors label or identify previously mentioned entities. This can range from explicit to implicit identification, including anaphora (using forms like "it", "she", "they") for highly accessible previous mentions to elaborate descriptions, especially in genres prone to using new and varied terms, such as scientific or specialized discourse, where the same concept might be referred to with different forms over the course of a text. The accessibility of a referent is not only influenced by the form of the referring expression itself but also by textual context and reader/viewer expectations (Miller and Garrod, 1982). The measured accessibility may vary significantly depending on these factors, meaning that static metrics like word repetition do not always fully reflect the dynamic cognitive processes of comprehension and re-identification of discourse entities. However, this relationship is not absolute and can be influenced by textual genre, authorial style, and the specific rhetorical strategies employed. For instance, skilled writers may use carefully crafted, detailed descriptions of a particular concept to signal a shift to discussing something new or nuanced about that concept, while more general or vague references may clump around central themes or entities that remain topics of conversation over multiple passages. Therefore, a measure of lexical cohesion that incorporates the dynamic interplay of referring expression length and informativeness can provide a richer insight into how a text manages its topical focus and transitions between ideas. We explore this hypothesis by introducing a proposed measure that calculates the informativeness and functional successfulness (in terms of degree of anaphora, self-reference, or non-reference type of relation, akin to notions discussed in Mann & Thompson, 1988) of referring expressions across a document. response: Automatic analysis of semantic similarity in comparable text through syntactic tree matching One of the central tasks in natural language processing today is the analysis of meaning and semantic similarity. This includes the challenging task of finding similarity between expressions in the natural language of various forms, be it sentences, phrases, or words. A particular and important case of this is the comparison of texts in questions such as "What is the translation of a given text sentence into a different language?" or "What does a given short text summary say (in simpler language) about the text it summarizes?". The latter question is very similar to the task of generating comparables (short summaries alongside a full text) in search results. In comparative linguistics studies on texts in different languages, the comparison is typically done with the help of dictionaries, glossaries, or bilingual lexicons. However, these methods have limitations, as among semantic relations beyond simple translation there can be many other types of relations - "Two sentences are paraphrases", "A short sentence summarizes a longer paragraph", or "Sentence 1 implies Sentence 2 and adds new information" - which cannot be captured rigidly by these traditional approaches. Furthermore, if we consider texts belonging to different domains or genres - say, a news article or a business report - translating the text would often be insufficient, if even applicable, to find similarity relations. For such different texts in the same language, we specifically wish to find semantic rather than textual similarity. In the literature on the acquisition and representation of meaning in computational models (formal semantics), the theory of "semantic similarity" or "meaning comparison" studies the formal (not necessarily computational) properties of expressions that can guarantee one expression can in principle be "interpreted" based on another, without necessarily being a translation or paraphrase. However, such formal treatment usually relies on formal language theory and would be hard to apply to natural language processing tasks that require scalable algorithms on large and diverse textual data. Our approach to analyzing semantic similarity in texts, especially within comparable texts side-by-side, focuses on exploiting the syntactic structure of the language. The idea is that semantically related expressions are likely to share common syntactic patterns, even if their surface forms appear very different. Specifically, given two comparable texts in the same language, we first build syntactic trees for both texts (using standard NLP parsing tools), and then attempt to match pairs of corresponding subtrees in the two trees. This task of syntactic tree matching, or more specifically, aligning syntactic trees, has been studied historically in translation and alignment tasks (Brown et al., 1993), but the focus there has almost entirely been on synchronizing words and their corresponding parts of speech across source and target. If we broaden the scope beyond just word-to-word alignment, we can match larger syntactic structures. For example, matching clauses or subclauses across comparable texts allows for capturing relations that go beyond word-level semantics. In previous studies (Miyao and Tsujii, 2000; Venturini, 1997), the task of finding these larger syntactic alignments from comparable texts has been approached with a focus on mostly youth syntax, given that, in comparative texts, the surface word orders can vary significantly between languages but the broader syntactic functional roles (between what we call arguments or complements of a verb) remain consistent. However, as observed by Pulman and Clark (2007), the method of comparing syntactic trees for semantic analysis carries over to monolingual texts within the same language: when a person clarifies or explains a sentence in a different way, the essential meaning is often preserved

response: Training natural language understanding (NLU) models for task-oriented dialogue systems using real conversation data is often challenging due to data scarcity. In particular, NLU modules are often trained on relatively small amounts of annotated data which may not fully cover the various linguistic phenomena and dialogues involved in the voice-user interface. A particular issue is the limited vocabulary and language expression – in face questions or commands asked by users may be expressed in a variety of ways and the models have to learn to understand these different expressions that have the same meaning (alternatives), or be able to generalize beyond what they observed during training. To overcome this data scarcity problem, we explore data augmentation techniques. Our aim is to generate diverse training samples to help NLU models to improve their understanding of natural language inputs. Sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models are a powerful tool for natural language generation and summarization. They can be used to generate alternative expressions based on sample from real conversations. Traditional Seq2Seq model only focuses on individual utterance without considering its relationship with other utterances in the same dialogue. In task-oriented dialogue systems, however, dialogues are sequential and thus semantically related. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to data augmentation by leveraging Seq2Seq model to generate other semantically equivalent or related sentences based on the same semantic goal of given context. One key contribution of our approach is that it includes a different aspect of the training corpus. Unlike traditional data augmentation methods, while the latter typically generate additional samples based on single examples, our approach uses the whole corpus to provide plausible alternative sentences. Our model generates an augmented dataset through analyzing how similar (in terms of semantic content) sentences vary in their syntactic structure, allowing it to model more different representations in the augmented dataset. We specifically incorporate a diversity rank mechanism in our Seq2Seq model. This mechanism compels the model to generate diverse utterances with respect to the candidates it has previously seen and the structure that they might represent. Further, to make our approach effective, we introduce a novel token-level embedding of dialogues. This embedding takes into account the nuances of dialogue structure and the fact that different matched pairs of interlocutor statements can express the same underlying meaning. For instance, "I'd like to find a vegetarian restaurant" and "Do you have any recommendations for places with vegetarian options?" convey the same meaning even though they use different words and structures. Our token-level embedding captures this semantic equivalence. Specifically, each utterance is embedded into a high-dimensional vector space, and we compute a similarity function between such embeddings to capture how synonymous or semantically similar two utterances are. This allows us to focus the diversity of our dataset generation almost entirely on functionally equivalent expression in the dialogue context. Prior work in NLU and data augmentation, including previous works using Seq2Seq models for data augmentation in general language understanding or task-oriented dialogue systems, does not incorporate this nuanced understanding of dialogue structure or semantic equivalence. We provide this novel approach with extensive experiments on two public datasets: the Airline Travel Information System dataset and a semantic frame annotation of the Stanford Multi-turn, Multi-domain Dialogue Dataset. Results show improvements in semantic understanding from the NLU model; on the target metric of F-score, improvements are 6.38 and 10.04 points respectively over the baseline models without augmentation. Furthermore, case studies are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. The case studies include real-world examples of diverse expressions, showing instances where our model learns to generate alternatives that better capture the diverse ways users might express similar ideas, improving generalization to untrained data. This paper contributes a methodology for data augmentation that uses an understanding of semantics under dialogue

However, natural language also features cases where arguments are syntactically absent (or only weakly present) but can still be inferred by the reader, e.g. “John got tickets for Mary and his mom”. In this context, the argument “John” is syntactically missing but can be inferred (e.g., as the “agent” of buying tickets, as the argument of “got”), though this inference is not “obvious” (for instance, due to verbs like “get” which do not always take explicit subjects, or because the expected subject is in a different sentence). This problem is called Implicit Argument Prediction (IAP) in the Sentiment Analysis (SA), Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Dependency Parsing (DP) domains (Das and Smith, 2017; Das et al., 2017; Reyes et al., 2018). In these cases, the missing arguments are semantically defined through the predicate (e.g., “buy” = “passive” implies buyers and buyers’ beneficiaries as arguments), and presumably or even definitely present in the text, so that this argument can be found somewhere in the text or in the wider narrative context (e.g., assuming Mary and his mom are assumed to buy the tickets for themselves). response: Certainly, here is my answer: Vision and language research has recently witnessed an explosion of interest, driven by the promise of systems that can understand and process visual content using language representations. This type of research has the potential to create various applications, including image-to-text translation, image captioning, visual question answering (VQA), and multimodal paraphrasing. However, one of the primary constraints that this area of research faces is the availability and quality of datasets that can be used for training and evaluating language models integrated with vision systems. In this paper, we undertake a review and analysis of existing datasets that have been developed for this purpose. Our aim is not only to provide an up-to-date, comprehensive list of such datasets but also to evaluate them based on various metrics, and discuss their strengths and weaknesses. We introduce a set of quality metrics that we propose to be among the most relevant for evaluating datasets in vision and language research. These metrics cover various aspects of the datasets including coverage (e.g., range of visual content, range of linguistic concepts and complexity), annotation standard, data consistency, and creative license given to annotators. These aspects are crucial because they influence the generalization capability and applicability of the models trained on these datasets. Our analysis reveals a diverse set of datasets covering different domains, modalities, and application scenarios. One of the trends we observe is that recent datasets tend to have more complex language and more abstract concepts, reflecting an increasing focus on 'understanding' and 'reasoning' over 'classification' tasks. However, there are notable differences in the strengths and weaknesses of each dataset. Some datasets are better suited to certain applications (e.g., captioning, VQA) due to the nature and extent of the annotations. For example, datasets with more complete, varied, and complex annotations tend to be more useful for model development that requires nuanced understanding of language. We categorize datasets into several groups based on our proposed metrics and the type of research they are designed to support. For instance, we have the 'captioning' datasets, which focus on generating textual descriptions of images or videos; the 'VQA' datasets that support research on answering questions about visual content; and datasets that support more abstract tasks such as multimodal paraphrasing or generation of informative image captions. This categorization not only helps in understanding the specific research questions or tasks that these datasets are designed to address but also highlights potential areas of overlap and complementarity among them. Another key aspect of our review is evaluating the influence of dataset characteristics on model performance and generalization ability. We discuss examples where the strengths and weaknesses of the datasets directly impact the models developed on them. For instance, a model trained on a dataset with very limited variation in language complexity and visual concepts may struggle when encountering real-world data with greater diversity. Conversely, datasets with more creative and varied annotations may lead to more flexible models that can generalise better across different application scenarios. We also reflect on the challenges faced by dataset designers and any emerging best practices for creating high-quality, effective datasets for vision and language research. This includes balancing the trade-offs between data volume, annotation complexity, and dataset cost, as well as considerations on data diversity, representativeness, and alignment with real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we highlight the importance of maintaining high-quality annotation standards, given the challenges of annotation consistency, inter-annotator agreement, and potential biases in the annotation process. We discuss the use of active learning techniques, iterative annotation refinements, and comprehensive review processes to address some of these issues. In conclusion, while there are many promising datasets available for vision and language research, there remains a gap between the complexity and nuance of real-world applications

response: Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Over the past four decades, the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has experienced rapid growth and development. Nevertheless, despite the deep advances in techniques and the wide range of applications that NLP technology can offer, there seems to be a particular barrier, often referred to as a "glass ceiling", that has limited the advancement and representation of certain groups within the field. In this paper, we provide empirical evidence based on a rigorously studied mathematical model for bi-populated networks that a glass ceiling within the field of NLP has developed since the mid 2000s. This barrier affects not only the demographic makeup of those contributing to, and participating in, the field, but also the adoption and implementation of certain types of research, despite their potential to advance our understanding of language and its processing. Historically, among the computational sciences, NLP has had a relatively strong presence of women and underrepresented minorities, perhaps due to its interdisciplinary nature that draws from linguistics, computer science, and cognitive psychology (Chierchia & McConnell-Ginet, 2000). The core idea of LTLM is the encoding of a sentence as a latent tree structure where nodes represent word roles. A particular word can occupy different roles depending on the context of the corresponding sentence. The role assignments encourage the embedding and generalization of syntactic and semantic relations between words. The model can represent abstract links that may not necessarily correspond to tree structures actually present in the language. Table 1 (left) outlines the major challenges of LTLM and ways to address them. The knowledge of language we want to model is inherently ambiguous and lazy retrieved – unlike many computer programs, verbal communication often makes implicit reference to shared context and prior knowledge. This ambiguity presents a challenge to any model aiming to encode the structure of language in a sample from a language distribution. Another difficulty we address is the fact that natural language structure is indefinitely pliable: any given sequence of words can be interpreted in countless ways, as much as it can be very unequivocal in its meaning. Our model approaches these challenges from multiple angles. Firstly, it employs Gibbs sampling to estimate the roles of the words in the given sentence. This sampling process is guided by the model's parameters that are learned through exposure to the training data. The process results in an assignment of roles that captures the intricate dependencies and patterns in the data in a way that a simple n-gram or even the most advanced n-gram model augmented by features or carefully selected word embeddings are unable to capture. We then take advantage of the tree structure learned during this sampling process to predict the next word as a combination of predicting the role of the next word and the contexts corresponding to that role. While the role assignments likely doesn’t represent a tangible, observable linguistic structure (and the structure that emerges might not correspond to any known linguistic typology), it allows the model to generalize over varied syntactic and semantic configurations. This flexibility of representation is particularly useful in resolving ambiguity and capturing the blurred boundaries between syntactically similar but semantically distinct sequences. Phrase structure questions have been tackled using context-free grammars (CFGs) and principled ways of making them more compact and tractable have been explored (Fraser and Hanson, 1990; Ratnaparkhi, 1997). However, due to the pervasive phenomena of word structure complexity in several natural languages, particularly those that are morphologically rich (but also many others) such as German, Dutch, Polish, and Russian (Haspelmath, 1996; Baker, 2001), context-free grammar (CFG) -based phrase structure parsing approaches that operate directly on words and use simple lexical descriptions of words have been found to be inadequate (Schmid, 2000). The problem of morphological richness in these languages can be traced back to issues in both the regularity and complexity of the structure of words. A simple word may have several derivations, so that this word can be represented as symbols appearing in several lexical rules. The different derivations may be shallowly related (but often assumed to be the same word in a syntactic context in a phrase structure grammar). response: Training parallel corpora is one of the key ingredients in statistical machine translation (SMT) (Koehn, 2005). Conventionally parallel corpora are collected from various public and proprietary sources (e.g., book translations), organizations (e.g., EU parliament proceedings), and specialized institutes (e.g., United Nations). For many language pairs, questions remain as to whether these traditional sources are sufficiently large for state-of-the-art SMT systems or "gold" enough to produce the best translations. There is of course the issue of domain overlap, i.e., texts coming from different domains can create out-of-domain characteristics that can deplete translation quality when trained on limited resources (Toral and Way, 2010;Bojar et al., 2011). Consequently, efforts have been made to enlarge existing parallel corpora by re-releasing the raw data, weighted boosting sample selection (Das and Smith, 2004), and web sources (Wubben et al., 2008). However, these approaches are still restricted to parallel sources and thus fail to expose the statistical MT system to larger volumes of in-domain training data. This paper introduces a novel approach to mine parallel sentences from the web or any other large scale text collections, using a combination of a carefully designed web search query and an automatic document alignment based approach. We present an initial empirical evaluation of this novel approach, while the system is still in its development stage. Striking substantial improvement over several baseline approaches, we identify the core variables responsible for these results and carefully analyze how distinct web mining approaches perform. The MT task focused in this study is limited to German-English translation. We believe, however, that the proposed mining methodology can be generalised to other language pairs and help to increase "in-domain" training data leading to stronger SMT systems. But it is not just "mining" that we investigate: we also examine the quality and adequacy of the obtained parallel data in SMT. We discuss general methods to evaluate measured variables such as lexical overlap, sentence level, and paraphrasing compatibility. The paper is structured as follows: we initially present the methodology and its rationale before we dive deep into the evaluation. We then describe the technical implementation of the entire system and the set up of the large-scale experimental evaluation. Finally, we analyze the evaluation results and draw conclusions that are both generalizable to other language/purpose pairs and specific to the German-English domain. Human communication would not function without the ability to refer, using both proper names and descriptive terms. Most current text generation technology, however, resorts to deterministic or relatively simplistic ways of producing REs, often relying on questions or status updates as basis for the content and often using only one form of referring expression (e.g., a proper name) to reference the same entity, even if the text is longer or includes multiple REs. While it is important that generated REs keeps changing as needed, it is also important to ensure that the variability in referring expressions, if any, is not interrupted in ways that seem to human readers as inexplicable and disruptive to the flow of the text. This paper presents an approach to text generation that produces REs that exhibit human-like variation in their form and continuity. The presented method follows from previous work on using statistical and machine learning models to generate human-like referring expressions (Jansen et al., 2009a; 2009b; Jansen and Weld, 2011; Lioutikov et al., 2013; Jansen et al., 2015). Specifically, it uses a statistical model to predict when a newly introduced concept (e.g., a character in a story) should be named rather than described, and what label to use if more than one is possible (i.e., the coreference model). It further extends this to create variation by using distinct (and equidistant) pseudonyms for the character as story progresses, using phonological variation to create in-story character names. This is key to the present study and a focus on this paper, which will highlight how model analysis yields insights into socio-linguistic variations and the computational analysis and generation of such. For this, we introduce variation models to highlight variation on all levels of expression (e.g., the choice of pronouns or proper names, or synonyms) and a method to create REs that keep referring to the same entity in a human-like manner yet with variation, even within very short texts. This phenomenon gives rise to a new task called mixed language modeling (Liu and Che, 2009; Zhang, 2011), questions such as "What is the most prevalent and useful way to perform POS tagging for words distributed randomly in a mixed language text?" and “How useful can English words help in Chinese language modelling?" urgently need to be answered. However, this task is very challenging due to the following reasons. First, due to the lack of large scale annotated mixed language corpus, it is hard to train a POS tagger for mixed texts. Second, even for English-only language, POS tagging is still an open problem (Zhang, 2011). As shown in table 1, English-only POS tagging still suffers from 8.2% error rate while most of the Chinese-only taggers have achieved more than 98% accuracy (Huang et al., 2012). For mixed text, the situation becomes even worse. As shown in table 2, English words in Chinese or mixed texts are often tagged as a single label, which is usually represented as symbols like “en”, “foreign”, “f”, or even just ignored. This kind of tagging only works for script/character label, but cannot assist English language modelling. For example, to build a model for translating English keywords to Chinese, we must perform POS tagging for English first. The most straightforward solution is to use an English-only POS tagger for the English in mixed texts, but for mixed texts, it is not always clear which words are English and which are Chinese. Moreover, even when the word doesn’t come from English, it may still have English spelling in Chinese input (e.g., “fan” for “fashion”) and if one just uses an English tagger or depends too much on lookup, one loses useful signals from Chinese context, which often provides a lot of clues about its position and function in the sentence. response: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has been shown to outperform traditional phrase-based systems by modeling the entire sentence as a joint probability distribution over source and target sentences (Sutskever et al., 2014;Bahdanau et al., 2015). While the NMT approach captures the sentence semantics better than its predecessors, questions remain as to whether and how NMT models could be equipped to leverage document-level contextual information, which can often significantly improve the quality of translations (Denkowski and Lavie, 2014;Graham and Neubig, 2017;Chen et al., 2016;Nguyen et al., 2017). Previous research has reported that incorporating contextual information into NMT can lead to improved performance. Sentence-level contextual features, derived directly from the source sentence before decoding, can be used to estimate the similarity between source sentences (Liu et al., 2017;Wang and Zhang, 2017;Jia et al., 2017a). Another line of work addresses the document-level context by including sentences in the document preceding the target sentence in the encoder or by using referential features (Wei et al., 2016;Tu et al., 2016;Yuan et al., 2017). These techniques typically use assumed context while the NMT models need to learn the appropriate way of using the contextual information to increase translation quality (Chen et al., 2017b;Sanchez et al., 2017). However, extracting, representing, and integrating document-level contextual information into the neural translation framework presents several challenges (1) An effective and efficient method must be employed to represent and highlight contextual information at the document level (2) The NMT model must learn how the document-level context might influence the translation and this can be unsuitable for global features such as word occurrence counts (Liu et al., 2016;Li et al., 2016) (3) The model should ideally learn to focus on useful parts of the document-level context by dynamically determining which parts are relevant for the translation and (4) The document-level attention mechanism should also respect the dependency structure within the document (Huang et al., 2016). Fortunately, attention mechanisms can be used to handle such issues in NMT. The attention mechanism (Bahdanau et al., 2015) in NMT focuses on the relevant words in the source sentence. Attention can be used to dynamically focus on different aspects of the source sentence during decoding. However, to capture document-level contexts, the attention mechanism needs a mechanism to focus on the relevant parts of the document or sentences. Our model integrates the hierarchical attention mechanism over the document structure into the standard NMT architecture. We also introduce a document-level soft alignment mechanism, which is used by the hierarchical attention to focus on the relevant parts of the document. We demonstrate that our model learns to capture document-level context dynamically during the translation and shows significant improvement over a strong baseline at document-level translation task. The results also show that both encoder and decoder benefit from better context capture which supports our intuition that the proposed hierarchical attention mechanism allows the NMT model to focus on relevant parts of the source document during translation. We evaluate our model using WMT English to German translation task. Our results show a solid improvement of 0.45 BLEU compared to the hidden state sharing baseline

In OI work up to this point, entities have typically been objects of events, such as "Apple is overpriced." or "Apple is a great company." (Here "Apple" is the entity and the prepositional phrase of "overpriced" or "a great company" is the event attributing qualities to "Apple"). This paper focuses on a task variant where opinions are expressed about events, and more specifically about events with effects on entities. For example, in the sentence "The Wall Street protests had a significant impact on financial regulation." (or " ... have had a negative impact ..."), the focus of the opinion is the "significant impact", an effect that has consequences for financial regulation. This subset of opinion inference problems is sometimes known as "effect event inference" or sometimes as "subject-verb-object inference with event extensions." The focus of this type of sentence is on the event and its effects, and the entities that those effects target or pertain to. A unit of Forth this task this is a specific type of MWE called an +/ -affect event (sometimes +/ -effect event)", reflecting that we are interested in events with positive and/or negative effects on the entities. The key to building systems for this type of OI stems from acquiring or analyzing a lexicon of such events. The fundamental task here is to determine for each word or word combination whether it can in principle be the object of a positive or negative opinion towards an entity and if so, which entities it "affects" when leading such opinions. For example, "affect" (positive or negative) could imply whether the event leads to an increase (positive) or decrease (negative) in value or the status or property of the entity measured by any aspect listed in a predefined set, e.g., reputation, public perception, market position, legal standing, skills or qualifications, etc. For each such event candidate, if detected, we need to identify which entities it can possibly affect - entities generally can refer to people (e.g., person, team, organization, or role – such as CEO, but also including phantom people/personifications like "the country") or non-persons (e.g., companies, public institutions, ideas/principles, locations, artifacts like software or physical products, abstract entities like government or society) and so on. An extensive and well-defined lexicon of such +/ -affect events would inherently enable a computational system to perform OI for sentences expressing opinions about effects. However, current NLP resources, including WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998), which is one of the most comprehensive and widely used lexical resources, are not equipped to handle this task directly. Most importantly, WordNet is a lexicon of terms, and users wanting to identify words or combinations thereof that reliably signal an event with an effect must face the issues of polysemy and homography. Polysemy is when a single term can represent multiple senses or meanings (e.g., "cool" can mean high temperature, fashionable, or very good), and homography, or word ambiguity, occurs when two words with different meanings are spelled the same (e.g., "bank" can be a financial institution or a river bank). These phenomena make it difficult to ascertain whether a term like "drain" could refer to a negative effect

The goal of bilingual sentence compression is not only to reduce the length of sentences while preserving or even enhancing their informational value within each language but also to produce parallel compressed sentences that are both linguistically consistent and semantically aligned across languages. This can be beneficial for multilingual NLP tasks such as cross-lingual text summarization, where the summarization model, based on the training in the source language, can benefit from parallel compressed sentences in the target language for ensuring consistency and avoiding discrepancies in generating summaries across languages. The problem is further exacerbated by domains like biology, medicine, or finance where knowledge often has to be integrated from multiple, domain-centric sources. Information Extraction (IE) is key to helping make sense of this vast body of knowledge. Traditional IE approaches rely on manual curation of large, domain-specific, and language-specific knowledge resources, questions scope and relevance. Open Information Extraction (OIE) aims to break down these restrictions by extracting "useful" sentences from large text corpora, using only the text itself and no pre-existing domain knowledge (Banken and McCallum, 2006). For this purpose, these systems view sentences as binary or unary "affects" or "relates" between two entities assumed to occupy the subject and object slots. However, OIE systems produce substantial amounts of noisy or semantically inappropriate extractions. For example, an OIE system might extract: "Peanuts have the shape of a pod." as an entity-entity relationship. While the text in itself may be correct, the extracted claim is of little use in a large-scale knowledge graph. The culprit behind such extraction errors doesn't come from the underlying algorithms themselves, but from the lack of input constraints to contextualize and validate the extractions. The core assumption of OIE systems is that the text itself should provide enough signal for the extractions, but a dependence on the text alone can be insufficient. Most current entity recognition systems can handle simple mention structures (e.g., "NIST was established in 1901 by Charles Edward Merriam"). However, the task becomes more challenging when mentions can contain other mentions recursively, forming a nested structure that may require inference and understanding of higher-level semantic relations. This paper focuses on the problem of detecting nested mention structures. For example, in the sentence "The U.S. President awards NIST's Samuel Morse award to the inventor of the telegraph Samuel Morse", the mention "Samuel Morse" is nested within the mention "NIST's Samuel Morse award". This nested structure cannot be derived directly from surface patterns but requires understanding of the context and related entities (such as the organization "NIST" and the individual "Samuel Morse"). Recent work on entity recognition indicates that the state-of-the-art systems (such as NER systems) can handle some types of nested mentions, but these systems are not specifically designed for deep hierarchical or recursive mention structures. For example, Spacy and CoreNLP, widely-used NLP libraries, perform well on entity recognition on standard datasets, but they may struggle with nested mention structures as in the above example. To specifically tackle nested mention recognition while maintaining scalability, we propose a neural transition-based model. In this model, we first align every mention with a structured representation called a "forest"; this forest consists of a collection of rooted trees (or "constituents") that represent the hierarchical structure of mentions in the sentence. For example, in the sentence "The U.S. President awards NIST's Samuel Morse award to the inventor of the telegraph Samuel Morse", the forest could contain two trees: "The U.S. President awards NIST's Samuel Morse award" and "inventor of the telegraph Samuel Morse". We then learn to build the forest's structure in a bottom-up manner through a series of action sequences. Each action can be thought of as a step in building or combining trees within the forest. For instance, an action might insinuate a new tree into the forest or merge a tree with another. We represent actions using a vector of attributes based on local context features (such as neighboring words and their predicted entities), and we learn these actions using a policy that is optimized over labeled training data. Crucial to our model is the use of Stack-LSTM to aggregate the information from the previous actions and the current state. Stack-LSTM is an extension of the traditional LSTM architecture that can efficiently and effectively capture and propagate information from long histories of states. Our system also incorporates a character-based component. While traditional word-level models use word embeddings, we complement these with character-level embeddings to capture typographic patterns that can be useful for identifying unique entity names and distinguishing between similar entities or typographic variations of the same entity. For instance, "Samuel Morse" and "Samuel M. Morse" may require these lower-level patterns to distinguish between them. These features have traditionally been manually designed to capture useful knowledge such as linguistic information, domain specific characteristics, and so on. Most of these feature sets have been incrementally developed for improving the translation quality, and thus, involve a fair amount of experimentation and clinical evaluation. Another way of constructing features for SMT is through the use of distributed representations (Benni, 2011;Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016). In particular, for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, distributed representations have been most commonly learned from knowledge bases or large text corpora using models such as word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013b) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014). These weighted vectors have shown advantages over traditional handcrafted features in many NLP tasks including machine translation (Marcobrandi et al., 2014;Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016;Zhang et al., 2016). However, it is often the case that these learned features can still benefit from further refinement or even transformation to better match the requirements of a given task. One way to further learn task-specific feature representations is through different training objectives or with shallow structures. In this paper, we focus on the idea of using Deep Auto-Encoders (DAEs) to learn features, not just for training shallow structured models, but as high-dimensional representations for deeper structured SMT models such as phrase-based models. The concept of using DAEs is not new. For example, Bengio et al. (2009) and Le et al. (2012) have proposed training unsupervised DAEs (often pre-trained with Deep Belief Nets [DBNs] Hinton et al., 2006) and using these representations as features for different tasks. Similarly, the DBN features together with additional transformations and refining, have been used for improving machine translation performance (Sun et al., 2016;Zhang et al., 2016). However, DBNs and DAEs are often considered for monolingual learning where large amounts of monolingual data are available. This paper extends the concept of deep learning features in a new direction by: (i) using DAEs for learning truly bilingual features, given the availability of zero shot data; (ii) further improving the learned features with semi-supervised fine-tuning. These learned features thus learn to encode the two languages jointly and use both parallel and monolingual data. response: Training GANs can be challenging due to modecollapse—a phenomenon where the generated outputs become too homogeneous. To alleviate this issue, multiple solutions have been proposed (Salimans et al., 2016; Che et al., 2017; Odena et al., 2016; Miyato et al., 2018; Romera et al., 2018). However, they often introduce extra computation or require hyperparameter tuning. In our work, we propose to utilize fractal filters (Adams et al., 2012), which keeps changing its resonant neurons with respect to its input. Through knowledge distillation, we transfer the knowledge from a powerful discriminator (captured by fractal filters) to a lightweight discriminator that only uses a fraction of parameters. This approach is surprisingly simple, yet effective. Unsupervised Learning of Quality Metrics from Discriminator Feedback - While we focus on supervised learning in this work, we hope to contribute ideas that can eventually extend to unsupervised configurations where a human assessor is not available. In such setups, the discriminator should learn to abstract good quality from samples without feedback. We explore this direction by studying how reward-driven learning within or outside the GAN framework affects the quality of generated samples. One potential direction could be incorporating auxiliary tasks, such as predicting ratings from the discriminator, which could guide the generator towards quality-centric generation. Exploring the landscape of such techniques and their interplay with our proposed approach is plausible for future research. Using Discriminator Feedback for Improved Stability - The fractal filters used in our discriminator are analyzed as an example of using feedback from the generator-discriminator interaction as a learning signal. The key insight is that, despite the noise inherent in adversarial loss, the diversity of responses from the discriminator can encode rich, sub-sensory-level features that guide the generator towards more contextual or relevant responses. Extending this idea, we design experiments where the discriminator targets different characteristics (e.g., measured by human preferences) and observe how the generator's quality evolves. For example, if the discriminator is trained to distinguish between "interesting" and "boring" responses, the generator should adapt to generate more informative samples. Model Interpretability and Feedback Analysis - We aim to provide insights into how the generative model learns from the discriminator. The fractal filters in our discriminator offer a readily interpretable view of what structure or features the model considers discriminative or essential for high-quality responses. This could serve as a bridge to studying model interpretability in GANs. Furthermore, detailed analysis of the feedback landscapes (how the discriminator's responses change with generated sample quality and generator updates) could provide heuristic rules for improving GAN training architectures. The key to our approach lies in a compositional discriminator that adapts dynamically to the generator's output and a reduced, yet effective, feedback mechanism that allows for efficient and stable training of the generator. We conclude that the proposed framework, which introduces a simpler yet more comprehensive way to use feedback from the discriminator, offers new avenues for improving quality metrics in generated samples. Further exploration across different datasets and conditions will help refine the impact of parameters like fractal filter size and the integration with auxiliary objectives. Such explorations could lead to better understanding of how to guide unsupervised models towards capturing high-quality representations of data, a challenge that remains central in many domains of generative neural networks. This work contributes toward that goal by offering a tangible method to harness discriminator feedback more effectively and systematically. Our work fills this gap by proposing a novel task - Anecdote Recognition and Recommendation. response: Training neural machine translation (NMT) models for low-resource language pairs (such as translating from X to Z or vice versa, where Z is a rare language and available training data is scarce) is notoriously challenging. This is because NMT models are data-hungry and require large amounts of parallel and monolingual data to learn relevant translation patterns. In practical settings, however, it is often possible to gather parallel data between rare language Z and a "rich" language Y that has large amounts of resources, but not between X and Z. Table 1 (not included in text format here) demonstrates how extensively less-resourced languages (like most non-English languages) are represented in publicly available parallel datasets. Even when there is some training data available for the rare language Z, such as translations from another rich language (e.g., English), using directly this available Z-X data to train a good NMT from X to Z can be challenging due to the inherent scarcity and potential sparsity of the data. Moreover, training NMT models directly from Z to X with very scarce data can also be problematic because of potential overfitting, especially considering that similar sentences in the training data may occur very infrequently or not at all. To address this problem, we propose a new training architecture for this context, which we term as Triangular Architecture for NMT (TA-NMT).
